title: A hundred pardons
hookLine: Bhishma tells the hall how Shishupala was born, and why Krishna once promised his mother a hundred pardons
carry: kshama: forbearance is a godly quality
last: ANGER CLOUDS THE MIND THAT SEES.

cards: The kings are muttering about war. Bhima has nearly leapt across the hall. Bhishma has been mocked to his face.
And the one person all of this is about just sits there, and hasn't said a word. So Bhishma, still holding Bhima's arm, does something unexpected. He stops the argument and tells a story.
If you want to understand this hall, he says in effect, you have to go back to the day Shishupala was born.

teach.b: Here's the story as Bhishma tells it. Shishupala was born in the royal house of Chedi with three eyes and four arms, and he cried out at birth with a strange, unearthly cry.
His frightened parents thought of giving him up. Then a voice came from no one they could see.
Don't abandon him. He will grow strong. His death is not yet.

teach.h: ON KRISHNA'S LAP, THE SIGNS FALL AWAY.
teach.b: And it told them how to know who would end his life: the one on whose lap the child's extra arms would fall away and his third eye would vanish. So the king and queen put the baby on the lap of every visitor.
King after king held him. Nothing happened.
Then Krishna came to visit his aunt, and the child was placed on his lap. The two extra arms fell away. The third eye sank into his forehead and was gone.
Now his mother knew whose hand would one day take her son's life, and she was Krishna's father's sister. She begged him for a boon: spare my son.
Krishna promised to pardon a hundred of Shishupala's offenses, even ones that deserved death. So that's what Krishna is doing in the hall. He isn't ignoring the insults.
He's counting them. His silence is a promise to his aunt, made over a cradle long ago, kept insult by insult.

Hinduism has a word for it: kshama, forbearance, patient forgiveness. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists the qualities of a godly nature, and kshama is among them. It isn't weakness, and it isn't failing to notice.
It's strength that chooses not to strike, for as long as a promise asks.

how: Kshama, forbearance, is listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita (16.3). Some storytellers and commentators use Shishupala's birth story to explain Krishna's patience in the hall, reading his silence as the keeping of a promise to his aunt.

o: a king cursed to lose his strength until reminded
the sage whose voice warned his parents at his birth
Krishna's cousin, pardoned a hundred times by a promise

games.q: the cradle in Chedi — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna ignored Shishupala's insults because he didn't care
he was keeping a promise to Shishupala's mother to pardon his offenses.
the extra arms fell away on Krishna's lap
that was the sign the voice had foretold.
Shishupala's parents gave him up at birth
an unseen voice told them not to abandon him.

games.q: you're Shishupala's mother. on Krishna's lap, your son's extra arms have just fallen away, and you know what it means. what do you do?
o: hide your son from Krishna forever.
ask Krishna for a boon to spare him.
games.why: she begs Krishna, her nephew, and he promises to pardon a hundred of her son's offenses.

practice: Think of someone it's hard to be patient with. See them clearly, without pretending what they did was fine.
Breathe in, and feel the strength it takes not to strike back; breathe out, and offer them a little kshama, one pardon, just for today.
If you pray, you can ask for that forbearance in your prayer; if not, simply hold the pardon in silence.

wordCard.voice: Shishupala. Born with three eyes and four arms, spared at his mother's plea, and pardoned by Krishna a hundred times by promise.

orig.note: Sanskrit kṣamā: forbearance, patient forgiveness, the virtue Krishna shows in the hall.

carryVoice: Your line: kshama: forbearance is a godly quality. A hundred pardons, and he's counting. Day seven hundred sixty-one, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Sisupala-badha Parva (Bhishma tells of Shishupala's birth, the voice, the signs vanishing on Krishna's lap, and Krishna's promise to pardon a hundred offenses)
Bhagavad Gita 16.1–3 (the divine qualities, kshama among them)
